title: Scale Significance
subtitle: Small causes are required by large effects

blocks.html: Astronomical scales are bewildering to human intuition. Billions of stars, billions of galaxies, and structure so large that measurements of distance and time blur together. The Milky Way is said to be about 100,000 lightyears across.

A lightyear is often introduced as the distance a beam of light can travel in a year. To imagine that, we think of light speed—in one second, circling the Earth seven times or reaching three-quarters of the way to the Moon. And we expand that second into a year. This is a stretch for any human imagination.

But a lightyear is not even a distance in the way we commonly understand that term, as a length of space between two points existing at the same time. It was Einstein, in 1905, who broke open the secret that times and distances are specific to unique three-dimensional reference frames. Hermann Minkowski followed his rationale to the conclusion that intuitive 3D space has no primitive existence at all. A division of four-dimensional spacetime into space and time arises only relative to a unique timelike observer.

And at large scales, the intuition really does break down. A lightyear does not act like a distance, but rather like a latency: the minimum time elapsed at point A before any signal sent from point B can be received.

With our Earth, once the center of the universe, relegated to an afterthought in its own Solar System (0.0003% by mass), and facing the reality that we cannot even see what is happening out there right now, it is easy to derive a sense of human smallness and insignificance.
I propose that this feeling is unjustified; it hides a logical error.
